card.name: Troika
card.tagline: A Russian folk dance imitating the prancing of a three-horse team pulling a carriage.
card.profile: Troika is a Russian performance dance that mimics the movement of a three-horse team pulling a carriage. Traditionally performed in groups of three, the dance involves intricate weaving patterns and circular movement. It has evolved from its 1948 stage debut into a staple of Russian ethnographic ensembles, with related forms found in Poland and among Cajun communities.
card.insight: In the 1948 choreography by Nadezhda Nadezhdina, the central dancer of the trio is 'ejected' at the end of the sequence to join the trio ahead, creating a continuous, shifting chain of dancers.

card.profile_long: The Troika is a traditional Russian dance that draws its name and movement vocabulary from the 'troika,' a carriage or sled pulled by a team of three horses. The dance is performed in groups of three, typically consisting of one man and two women, though other gender combinations have been developed in later choreographies. The movement is designed to imitate the prancing of the horses as they pull a carriage. The dance is structured around a series of repeating phases performed in a circular formation, with the trios moving in a counter-clockwise direction. The first version of the dance for the stage was created by choreographer Nadezhda Nadezhdina in 1948 for the Beryozka ensemble. Since its introduction, the dance has become a standard part of the repertoire for virtually all Russian ethnographic dance ensembles. The structure of the dance is highly consistent, often divided into four distinct phases that repeat until the end of the musical piece. These phases include a trotting movement in a circle, a sequence of arm arches where dancers pass under each other's arms, and a circular round that rotates in both clockwise and counter-clockwise directions. A signature element of the dance involves the central dancer being 'ejected' at the end of the sequence to join the trio positioned immediately in front of them, ensuring the dance remains a continuous, shifting flow. Beyond Russia, the dance has parallels in other Slavic traditions, such as the Polish Trojak, and a version exists within the Cajun dance tradition, which some suggest may have originated when Russian Cossacks were stationed in Paris. A German contra dance known as the triolet, recorded in 1829, also features a similar trio structure of one man and two women. The dance serves as a performance piece that connects historical Russian transport imagery with a structured, social, and rhythmic group performance.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance was first created for the stage by choreographer Nadezhda Nadezhdina for the Beryozka folklore dance troupe in 1948. It is based on traditional Russian folk dances and the imagery of a three-horse team.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers form groups of three, arranged in a circle. The dance consists of four phases: first, the trios trot in a circle holding hands; second, the center dancer raises their arms to allow the partners to pass under; third, the trio forms a round and rotates clockwise; fourth, the round rotates counter-clockwise, and the center dancer moves forward to join the next trio.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance symbolizes the three-horse team used by noble families to pull their carriages.
sections.notable_figures: Nadezhda Nadezhdina, who created the first version for the Beryozka troupe in 1948.
sections.regional_variants: Polish Trojak, Cajun Troika, and the German contra dance triolet (1829).
sections.lineage: Russian folk dance, specifically categorized as a Russian concert folk dance.
